schools.summary: Clarke calls this the last attack on Job, with Bildad practically owning himself and his companions worsted, mapping the little speech (dominion, armies, providence, then man's impurity); Wesley: Bildad answers Job's censure of God, the two sides having converged.
Henry commends Bildad's silence as contending for truth not victory, one who knew when he had said enough and would not wrangle for the last word.

Ellicott: Bildad attempts no formal reply but falls back on the position twice assumed by Eliphaz (4:17-21; 15:14-16) and once allowed by Job (14:4), implying his impiety in maintaining his righteousness.
Gill: Bildad seeks not to disprove Job but only to possess his mind with the majesty of God, to deter him from applying to God in a judicial way.

debates.question: Why is Bildad's third speech so brief?

sides.position: the dispute had narrowed until friends and Job scarcely differed, so Bildad let it drop, contending for truth not victory
Bildad and the friends were worsted in argument and had little left to say
Bildad meant not to argue at all but to overawe Job with God's majesty and deter his judicial appeal

themes: man cannot be just with God

schools.summary: Ellicott: God absolute in sovereignty and terrible in power, maintaining peace among his celestial hosts; Keil and Delitzsch pass on Schultens's verdict that the speech is a signal for retreat not battle, reduce it to two commonplaces, and parse 'dominion' as an infinitive absolute used as a noun.

Clarke: God an absolute sovereign whose fear is on all heaven's hosts, establishing order in the eternal world; Wesley: sovereign power and terror, the angels and stars keeping the peaceable order God appointed.
Gill fixes the subject as God, not man (against Sephorno): a universal, absolute, everlasting dominion, the 'fear' being not a fear God feels but the terror he inspires.

themes: the order of angels and stars

schools.summary: Clarke: innumerable troops, all creatures instruments of help or destruction, and the light of universal providence (sun on evil and good); Wesley: the hosts of angels and stars, the light a faint resemblance of God's care and bounty.
Gill spreads the muster wide: the angelic host and the stars in heaven, and on earth all creatures down to the frogs, lice, flies, and locusts that warred on Pharaoh.
Ellicott: the angels do but reflect God's dispensed glory, so it is hopeless for man, unclean from birth (Ps. 51:5), to think he can rival God's purity.

themes: the host of heaven and earth
the borrowed glory of the angels

schools.summary: Clarke: the question is no conclusion from Bildad's premises and unanswerable then but by the Gospel, man justified by faith in Christ's atonement and cleansed by grace; Wesley: 'man' is the miserable, sinful creature who should not quarrel with the dominion the angels submit to.
Gill grants no man is justified in himself, but says Bildad mistook Job, who sought the justification of his cause and clearing from hypocrisy, not the justification of his person as sinless.
Keil and Delitzsch give the plain rendering, setting the verse at the head of the descent from the mortal born of woman down through moon and stars to the worm.

themes: clean that is born of a woman

schools.summary: Clarke finds the impurity intrinsic: the moon ever changing, waxing and waning, spotted, its changeableness no match for God's unchanging nature; Wesley: the moon without lustre beside the Divine Majesty, the sun included by implication.
Gill reads the impurity as relative: the heavens lose all lustre only when compared with the Divine Being.
Henry: the lights shine not by reason of the glory which excelleth (a candle in sunlight, Isa. 24:23), yet God sees spots in them we never see, as he might in Job.
Ellicott: the stars are not clean before God because they rise and set, and the moon hides her face once every month.

debates.question: In what sense are the moon and stars 'not pure' before God?

sides.position: only relatively, outshone by a greater glory
intrinsically, being changeable and spotted, rising and setting

outliers.note: Raises and then sets aside the reading that 'stars' means the angels who kept not their first estate ('may be so, but I cannot see it in the text'), and judges Bildad's whole speech confused, inconclusive, and falsely reasoned.

schools.summary: Gill unfolds man the worm, of the earth, impure, weak, and mean, yet notes Christ was content to be called a worm (Ps. 22:6); without Christ's righteousness man makes a contemptible figure in heaven's court.

Clarke works the Hebrew (enosh, rimmah, toleah the maggot, per Parkhurst), the versions' 'man is corruption,' and the Targum's 'in his life a reptile, in his death a worm,' then marks Bildad ending confounded, incoherent, and abrupt.
Ellicott sets the verse beside its kindred, Ps. 8:4, Ps. 22:6, and Isa. 41:14 ('thou worm Jacob').

themes: man corruption, son of man a worm
